clue.text: There is no way to make a cut holding a weapon with no tip

indicators.note: A hand that holds something encloses it, so the cut word closes round the letter named beside it.
A tip is the pointed end, and a weapon's point is the letter it starts with — that one is gone.

parts.note: to notch something is to make a cut in it
the bare article, taken from in front of the weapon and slipped inside
the weapon is a LANCE, minus the L at its point

explanation.surface: You cannot slash at anybody while the weapon in your grip has had its point taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A weapon' reads as one phrase and the setter uses it as two: the article goes inside the cut, and what is left over is a lance.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Not a chance' is the flat refusal you snap at an impossible suggestion, which is what 'there is no way' says at greater length.

clue.text: Part of speech given by The Sound of Music extra accepting Oscar

indicators.note: To accept something is to take it in, so the word before this opens up and lets the next letter sit inside.

parts.note: the abbey scenes in that film are crowded with them, so an extra on that set is one
O is Oscar in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A bit-part player from the Sound of Music collecting an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar is the gold statuette in the surface and the radio alphabet's O in the wordplay, and the film title keeps both readings looking like showbusiness.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun is one of the classes grammar sorts words into, so the definition names it by membership of that set rather than by what it does.

clue.text: Spruce in yard — it shot up

indicators.note: Shooting up is movement from the bottom towards the top, and a down entry read upwards runs from its last letter back to its first.

parts.note: YD is the short form of a yard on any tape measure
the word goes in as it stands, two letters straight off the page

explanation.surface: A young conifer planted in a yard that has suddenly put on height.
explanation.walkthrough: Spruce is the tree in the picture and an adjective in the answer — smart and well turned out. The dash works as a semicolon, keeping 'it' apart from the yard it seems to belong to.
explanation.definitionFit: To be spruce is to be neat and trim, the same orderliness applied to how a person looks rather than to a room.

clue.text: The cable car travels across Norway with complete freedom

indicators.note: What travels does not stay where it was put, and these letters end up somewhere else entirely.
Travelling across a country takes that country in on the way, so its letter joins the ones being moved.

parts.note: eleven of the twelve letters, article and all
N is Norway's international vehicle code, and it supplies the twelfth letter

explanation.surface: A cable car crossing the Norwegian mountains, going wherever it pleases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' looks like the article introducing the cable car and is three of the letters you need, which is why the count seems short until you include it.
explanation.definitionFit: Carte blanche is the blank sheet you sign and hand over for someone else to fill in, so in English it names permission with no limits attached.

clue.text: Swimming in tears, becoming more nervous

indicators.note: Something swimming is adrift in liquid and free to turn any way it likes, which is what happens to the letters beside it.

parts.note: seven letters to be rearranged, the little word included

explanation.surface: Somebody weeping and growing steadily more jittery about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Antsy comes from having ants in your pants, so the comparative looks odd written down and is perfectly ordinary said aloud. 'In tears' is fodder, not a state anyone is in.
explanation.definitionFit: Antsy means fidgety and on edge, so its comparative covers anyone growing more nervous than they already were.

clue.text: Sausage from Australia one served up after work ended early

indicators.note: Serving something up sends it upwards to the table, and upwards in a down entry means reading the letters from the bottom.

parts.note: a CHORE is a piece of work, stopped one letter short

indicators.note: 'After' means later in the answer, so the piece it introduces is the one that goes in front.
A word ended early stops before its final letter, which is dropped rather than moved.

parts.note: OZ is the everyday nickname for Australia, spelled the way Aus is said
I is one, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A spicy sausage brought over from Australia and handed round once the shift finished early.
explanation.walkthrough: The sausage is Spanish, so naming Australia in the same breath is deliberate misdirection: the country is only in the clue for its two-letter nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: A chorizo is the paprika-spiced pork sausage of Spain, so 'sausage' defines it by class and leaves the wordplay to say which one.

clue.text: Little one eating hot fish

indicators.note: What gets eaten ends up inside the eater, so the short word closes round the letter that follows it.

parts.note: a cub is a little one — any young animal
H is the tap marked hot, a standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A small child getting through a plate of hot fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last and least interesting word in the sentence, which is how it hides. A chub is a fat, blunt-headed fish of the carp family, common in English rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: A chub is a thickset freshwater fish of the carp family, so 'fish' defines it by class, with nothing in it to narrow which one.

clue.text: Hot dog prepared with last of vegetable fat mixture

indicators.note: with means the rearranged dog letters are accompanied by the final letter, placed straight after them

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

indicators.note: prepared means made ready in a new form, so the letters of dog are rearranged
last of means the final letter of the word vegetable

parts.note: the last letter of vegetable is E
podge is informal British for excess body fat, as in a podgy person

explanation.surface: A recipe: a hot dog cooked with the end of a vegetable and some fat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot dog' reads as a snack, but the two words split: only 'dog' is rearranged by 'prepared', and 'fat' is a British noun for flab, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A hodgepodge is a confused jumble of different things, so it is a synonym of a mixture.

clue.text: Somehow heads across city's east side with many cycling

indicators.note: across means the heads word stretches across the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: beans is slang for heads, as in 'use your bean'

indicators.note: east side means the right-hand end, the last letter of the word city

parts.note: the last letter of city is Y

indicators.note: cycling means a letter of many is moved from one end to the other, the M going round to the back

explanation.surface: Somehow people head across to the eastern side of a city, many of them on bikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads' is slang here, not a verb, and the east side of a word in an across-style reading is its last letter; 'cycling' moves the first letter of many round to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: By any means is an idiom meaning in whatever way is possible, so it stands in for somehow.

clue.text: French and German articles written by Rose and Roger

parts.note: UN is the French indefinite article
DER is the masculine definite article in German
rose in the sense of got to his feet

explanation.surface: A pair of grammar pieces written up by two people called Rose and Roger.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger is a name in the surface and radio shorthand in the answer, the reply that confirms a message got through. Two capitalised first names are all that hold the sentence together.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Roger' is the radio operator's acknowledgement of a message received, so it stands in for exactly the word it means.

clue.text: Some included Dahl's old tales

definitions.note: The Edda is a single collection of Norse poems, so the plural 'tales' names the stories inside it rather than the book itself.

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part rather than the whole, so what is wanted is a run of letters sitting inside the words that follow.

parts.note: four letters in a row, starting near the end of the first word and crossing the gap into the name

explanation.surface: An anthology that takes in a few of Roald Dahl's earlier stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Included' looks like the hiding instruction and is carrier text holding half the letters, while the small word in front does all the instructing. The Edda are the Old Norse poems the Icelandic sagas grew out of.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edda is the pair of Icelandic books carrying the Norse myths, so 'old tales' points at the stories they hold.

clue.text: Defenceless targets police trap including one that initially escapes

indicators.note: What is included is taken inside, so the trap word opens and admits the letters named next into its middle.

parts.note: a sting is the operation police set up to catch someone
I is one, the Roman numeral

indicators.note: 'Initially' asks for the state of a word at its start, which here is just the letter it opens with.

parts.note: the opening letter of THAT, taken as the word stands
to duck a thing is to escape it by dodging

explanation.surface: Police set a trap and one of the people they were after slips out of it straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One that' reads as a person in the surface and is two separate letters in the wordplay, which is what makes the sting look like a whole story instead of a five-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: A sitting duck is a bird on the water that cannot get airborne, so the phrase names anyone who can be picked off without a fight.

clue.text: Clearly identify evil criminal

indicators.note: A criminal is bent, and letters described as bent do not keep the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: twelve letters, the whole of the fodder and the whole of the middle of the clue

explanation.surface: An instruction to name the wrongdoer and leave no doubt about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the middle two are the letters: 'criminal' arrives last, reading as the thing to be identified while doing the instructing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something settled definitively is settled beyond argument, and 'clearly' carries that same sense of leaving no room for doubt.

clue.text: Start of short emotional film tackling connection and love

indicators.note: 'Start of' takes the word after it at its very beginning, one letter and no more.

parts.note: the opening letter of SHORT

indicators.note: To tackle a thing is to get your arms round it, so the longer word wraps itself over the letters that follow.

parts.note: a weepie is a film made to bring the tears on
a tie is a connection between two people or things

explanation.surface: The opening of a brief tearjerker about a relationship and romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' arrives at the end reading as one more thing the film is about, and it is the definition — the affectionate name for a person rather than the feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetie-pie is what you call someone you dote on, and 'love' is the same term of endearment used as a noun for the person.

clue.text: Struggle with wordplay for 'floral'?

parts.note: read as a cryptic instruction, the answer's words say set the letters of 'for all' free, and freeing them into a new order gives floral

explanation.surface: Someone grapples with the wordplay for a flowery word.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is itself a little clue for 'floral': FREE signals an anagram of FOR ALL. A free-for-all is a chaotic fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A free-for-all is a disorganised brawl or contest open to anyone, so it is a struggle or melee.

clue.text: Small bird found in whiskey barrel at sea

indicators.note: Anything at sea is adrift with no fixed position, so the letters in front of it settle in a new order.

parts.note: W is whiskey in the radio alphabet — the spelling with the E is the giveaway
the other six letters of the fodder, handed over intact

explanation.surface: A little bird discovered inside a whiskey cask floating out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in' looks like the marker for a concealed answer, and nothing runs consecutively inside 'whiskey barrel' — it is joinery, and the instruction is the two words at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A warbler is any of the small songbirds named for their warbling, so the definition places it by size and class at once.

clue.text: Discovered your book about origin of Coriolis effect

indicators.note: discovered means uncovered, so the word your loses its outer letters, its cover

parts.note: your without its first and last letters is OU

indicators.note: about means going around, so the book word encloses the next letter

parts.note: a tome is a large book

indicators.note: origin of means the first letter of the word Coriolis

parts.note: the first letter of Coriolis is C

explanation.surface: Someone discovered a textbook about the Coriolis effect, the deflection of moving air on a spinning Earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' looks like found, but it means uncovered: the word your loses its cover at both ends. 'Coriolis effect' is a real phrase, which hides that 'effect' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome is a result or consequence, so it is a synonym of effect in the noun sense.

clue.text: Outside wanting kiss that's endless

indicators.note: To be wanting a thing is to be without it, so whatever is named next is missing from the longer word.

parts.note: external is the adjective meaning outside
a kiss is written X at the foot of a letter, and that X is the one taken out

explanation.surface: A person shut outside, longing for a kiss that would never have to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' sits where a deletion instruction usually sits and is the definition instead. The letter that actually goes is nowhere near either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal means having no end, so 'endless' is a plain synonym — the everyday word for the same absence of a stopping point.

clue.text: Ronald's cooking some bacon

definitions.note: Bacon is a mass noun and lardons are countable strips cut from it, so the definition names the stuff where the answer names the pieces.

indicators.note: Cooking turns ingredients into something other than what went in, and here the letters come out in a new arrangement.

parts.note: the name and its S together, seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Ronald at the stove with a pan of bacon on the go.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe reads as a possessive and is only there to lend its S to the fodder, which is why the name looks a letter short of what the count needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Lardons are the small strips of fat bacon a French recipe has you fry off, so 'some bacon' names them by what they are cut from.

clue.text: 12 keeping horse in shape

indicators.note: Keeping a thing means holding on to it inside, so the first word shuts round the letters that follow.

parts.note: twelve on the clock is noon
a nag is a worn-out horse

explanation.surface: Somebody's midday routine keeping a horse fit.
explanation.walkthrough: A bare number in a Guardian clue usually cross-refers to another entry, and that is the false trail here: this 12 is the hour on a clock face.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonagon is the nine-sided figure, so 'shape' defines it by class in geometry's plainest possible word.

clue.text: Gas upset baby

parts.note: neon is the gas in the tube of a bright sign
what ate at somebody upset them — the past tense of eat in that sense

explanation.surface: Wind troubling a very small baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' sits where a turnaround instruction would sit in a down clue and is a straight synonym: what ate at you is what upset you.
explanation.definitionFit: A neonate is a newborn in medical language, so 'baby' is the everyday word for the same person at the same age.

clue.text: That is horrid news to broadcast

indicators.note: Broadcasting is the farmer's word for scattering seed by hand, so what it touches lands anywhere at all.

parts.note: twelve letters, and the small word at the end is two of them

explanation.surface: A newsreader handed a grim bulletin to put out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like the join between the news and the broadcasting of it, which is why the count comes up two short for anyone who leaves it out.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In other words' announces a restatement, which is the job 'that is' does — the English of i.e., said the long way round.

clue.text: Something growing in street

indicators.note: The plainest hiding word there is: what is in the street is inside the word too, letter for letter and in order.

parts.note: four letters in a row, starting one letter in and stopping one short of the end

explanation.surface: A plant coming up somewhere along a road.
explanation.walkthrough: One small word carries the whole instruction, and it is so ordinary that most solvers read straight past it hunting for a mechanism elsewhere in five words.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition names the answer by class and no further: a tree is the thing you point at when you say something is growing there.

clue.text: Leaders of private schools start to pay attention

indicators.note: A leader stands at the front of the column, so what is wanted is the front letter of each word that follows.

parts.note: the opening letters of four consecutive words

explanation.surface: Fee-paying heads beginning to take notice of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials run through four words, and two of them are words the eye skips: 'start' and 'to' read as part of the definition and are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Psst' is the hiss you make to get somebody to look your way, so the definition gives what it means rather than what it says.

clue.text: Summit talks shunning both sides

indicators.note: shunning both sides means the word loses its first and last letters, keeping the middle

parts.note: speaks means talks

explanation.surface: A summit meeting where the talks are avoided by both opposing parties.
explanation.walkthrough: SPEAKS loses the S at each side. 'Summit' suggests a diplomatic conference, but it is the top of a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: A peak is the pointed top of a mountain, so it is a synonym of summit in its geographical sense.

clue.text: Parts of speech?

definitions.meaning: the grammarian's sense comes first: the categories a schoolchild lists off, noun and verb and adjective
the question mark withdraws that reading and asks for parts of the body instead — the two folds in the larynx that vibrate when you talk

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson asking you to name the categories that words fall into.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 down uses the same phrase in the grammar sense in the same grid, so the setter has clued it both ways: here it is anatomy, and there it is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech is made by air setting two folds of tissue in the larynx vibrating, so they are literally the parts that produce it.

clue.text: Look back across lake to find slender swimmers

indicators.note: A backward look reverses direction, and an across entry read backwards runs right to left.
Lying across a thing covers it, so the turned-round word spreads over the letter it is given to hold.

parts.note: to look is to see
L is the standard map abbreviation for a lake

explanation.surface: Glancing back over a lake and spotting something long and thin in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look back across lake' paints one glance over the water and every word in it is an instruction — the definition does not begin until 'slender'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eels are long, thin fish, so 'slender swimmers' describes them by shape and habit without naming the species.

clue.text: Jack and Jenny excited to tackle beginning of maths test

parts.note: a jack is a male donkey and a jenny a female, so the pair are asses

indicators.note: to tackle means to take hold of, so the excited word grips the next letter inside it

parts.note: sent is old slang for thrilled or excited, as in 'that music sends me'

indicators.note: beginning of means the first letter of the word maths

parts.note: the first letter of maths is M

explanation.surface: Two children, Jack and Jenny, are excited to take on a maths exam.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack and Jenny look like two pupils, but they are male and female donkeys. SENT 'tackles' M, the 'beginning of maths', after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessment is an evaluation of someone's ability, such as an exam, so it is a test.
